\chapter{In Order To, and Being Able}
\label{ch:ka-in-order-to}
\hlchaptermodality{73}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say why I am doing something, say what I can do, and say a instead of the.}

Complete KA-C73-a-flower and say all four dative-frame sentences in a row.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tumbā]{\kn{ತುಂಬಾ} (tumbā) — very}

\label{lesson:KA-C73-very}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say which of two drinks you prefer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ತುಂಬಾ}}
\textbf{\kn{ತುಂಬಾ}} (\emph{tumbā}) — \textquotedblleft{}very, a lot\textquotedblright{}.

You have had \kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು} (\emph{heccu}, \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{}) and \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ} (\emph{svalpa}, \textquotedblleft{}a little\textquotedblright{}) since the short-replies chapter, but only as answers to an offer — more rice, a little sugar. Neither of them can go in front of an adjective. \kn{ತುಂಬಾ} can, and that is the job it is here for.

\textbf{\kn{ತುಂಬಾ} \kn{ದೊಡ್ಡ}} (\emph{tumbā doḍḍa}) — \textquotedblleft{}very big.\textquotedblright{} It stands in front of the adjective, and the adjective still stands in front of the noun, unchanged, the way every Kannada adjective does.

It also works on its own as an answer, meaning \textquotedblleft{}a lot\textquotedblright{}, and it is the everyday way to say thank you warmly: \kn{ತುಂಬಾ} \kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Every adjective in this book, turned up. Six adjectives times one intensifier is twelve things you can now say about a thing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tumbā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tumbā doḍḍa}
  \item \emph{Say it:} put \emph{tumbā} in front of every adjective you remember
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{svalpa}, then \emph{heccu}, then \emph{tumbā}, and say which one goes with an adjective
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{\kn{ೂ}} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bandāga} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{kuttige}, \emph{āru}, \emph{aidu}, \emph{nālku}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ತುಂಬಾ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}very\textquotedblright{}.) Where does it go — before or after the adjective? (Before.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ōdalu]{\kn{ಓದಲು} (ōdalu) — in order to read}

\label{lesson:KA-C73-in-order-to}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what does \emph{tumbā} do to an adjective?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಓದಲು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಓದಲು}} (\emph{ōdalu}) — \textquotedblleft{}to read\textquotedblright{}, in the sense of \textquotedblleft{}in order to read\textquotedblright{}.

It is \kn{ಓದು} (\textquotedblleft{}to read\textquotedblright{}) with \textbf{-\kn{ಅಲು}} (\emph{-alu}) in place of its ending. That is the whole change, and it turns a verb into a purpose.

\textbf{\kn{ಪುಸ್ತಕ} \kn{ಓದಲು} \kn{ಹೋಗುತ್ತೇನೆ}} (\emph{pustaka ōdalu hōguttēne}) — \textquotedblleft{}I am going to read a book\textquotedblright{}, meaning I am going in order to read one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three endings, three ways to join two actions}]
The purpose comes before the verb it serves, like the when-clause did. Kannada builds a sentence by stacking what leads up to the action in front of it and putting the finished verb last, every time.

So you have now met three ways to hang one verb off another, and all three are endings rather than words: \textbf{-\kn{ಇ}} for \textquotedblleft{}having done it\textquotedblright{}, \textbf{-\kn{ಆಗ}} for \textquotedblleft{}at the time of doing it\textquotedblright{}, and \textbf{-\kn{ಅಲು}} for \textquotedblleft{}in order to do it\textquotedblright{}. English needs \emph{and}, \emph{when} and \emph{to} for those three; Kannada needs three shapes of one verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A reason to do something, said as part of the same sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ōdu}, then \emph{ōdalu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pustaka ōdalu hōguttēne}
  \item \emph{Say it:} take another verb you know and put \emph{-alu} on it
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bandāga}, and say what its ending means
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gottā} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nanage cahā bēku} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{bennu}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending means \textquotedblleft{}in order to\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{-\kn{ಅಲು}}.) Does the purpose come before or after the main verb? (Before.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭa]{\kn{ಟ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S151-letter-tta}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಜ} — and what does meeting it usually tell you about where a word came from?

One character this time — the last new one in this book so far, and one you have read inside a dozen everyday words.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಟ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಟ}} — \emph{ṭa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{t}, it is \textbf{ṭa} — the one made with the tongue curled back, which is a different letter from the \kn{ತ} you already trace and a different sound to a Kannada ear.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ಟ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಬಟ್ಟೆ}} \emph{baṭṭe} — cloth
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ}} \emph{beṭṭa} — a hill
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹೊಟ್ಟೆ}} \emph{hoṭṭe} — the stomach
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಊಟ}} \emph{ūṭa} — a meal
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಟ}}
Put your pen on \kn{ಟ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ಟ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಬಟ್ಟೆ}  ·  \kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ}  ·  \kn{ಊಟ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಟ} three times, saying \emph{ṭa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ಟ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಟ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ṭa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nanage kannaḍa baruttade]{\kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಕನ್ನಡ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತದೆ} (nanage kannaḍa baruttade) — I can speak Kannada}

\label{lesson:KA-C73-can}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which character did you trace last, and what does \emph{ōdalu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಕನ್ನಡ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತದೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಕನ್ನಡ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತದೆ}} (\emph{nanage kannaḍa baruttade}) — \textquotedblleft{}I can speak Kannada.\textquotedblright{}

The verb in it is \kn{ಬರು}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}. Read literally the sentence says \textquotedblleft{}to me, Kannada comes\textquotedblright{} — and that is exactly how Kannada says somebody can do something. A skill is not held; it arrives.

You already say \textbf{\kn{ನಾನು} \kn{ಕನ್ನಡ} \kn{ಮಾತನಾಡುತ್ತೇನೆ}} (\textquotedblleft{}I speak Kannada\textquotedblright{}). That reports what you do. This one reports what you can do, and it is the sentence a stranger asks you for.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the fourth thing the dative frame carries}]
Notice which frame it uses. \kn{ನನಗೆ} … \kn{ಬರುತ್ತದೆ} is the dative sentence again, the third thing you have poured into it: \kn{ನನಗೆ} \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು} for knowing, \kn{ನನಗೆ} … \kn{ಇಷ್ಟ} for liking, \kn{ನನಗೆ} … \kn{ಬೇಕು} for wanting, and now \kn{ನನಗೆ} … \kn{ಬರುತ್ತದೆ} for being able.

Four of the sentences a beginner needs most are one shape with one word swapped, and none of them has a subject in the English sense. Kannada puts the person in the dative and lets the thing be the subject, because knowing, liking, wanting and being able are all things that happen to you.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Say what you can do — and notice you have been building it all along.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nanage kannaḍa baruttade}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nanage kannaḍa gottu}, then \emph{nanage kannaḍa baruttade}, and say how they differ
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four dative sentences in a row
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ōdalu}, then use it in a sentence
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{alvā} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yāke} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{\kn{ಜ}} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nimage kāphi iṣṭavā} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{bhuja}, \emph{tuṭi}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb does Kannada use for being able? (\emph{baru}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}.) Say that you can speak Kannada.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ondu hūvu]{\kn{ಒಂದು} \kn{ಹೂವು} (ondu hūvu) — a flower}

\label{lesson:KA-C73-a-flower}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say that you can speak Kannada, and name the frame it uses.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಒಂದು} \kn{ಹೂವು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು} \kn{ಹೂವು}} (\emph{ondu hūvu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಒಂದು} has been the number one since the counting chapter. Put it in front of a noun when you are not counting anything and it stops being a number: it becomes the English \emph{a}.

Kannada has no article at all, and a bare \kn{ಹೂವು} is perfectly good on its own — it can mean \textquotedblleft{}the flower\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}flowers\textquotedblright{}, and which one it is comes from the situation. What \kn{ಒಂದು} adds is \emph{one particular one, not any special one}: you put it in when you would say \emph{a} in English and want the difference heard.

You have already used the same word for the opposite job in \kn{ಇನ್ನೊಂದು}, \textquotedblleft{}one more\textquotedblright{} — the counting sense still alive inside it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The last piece: a way to say \emph{a}. Between this and the pointing words you have had for a while, you can now say \textquotedblleft{}this flower\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}that flower\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}, which is the whole of what an article does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ondu hūvu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hūvu}, then \emph{ondu hūvu}, then \emph{innondu hūvu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} put \emph{ondu} in front of three nouns you know
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tumbā doḍḍa}, then \emph{ōdalu}, then \emph{nanage kannaḍa baruttade}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the whole chapter — \emph{tumbā}, \emph{ōdalu}, \emph{\kn{ಟ}}, \emph{nanage kannaḍa baruttade}, and this one
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{\kn{ಲ}} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nanage cahā iṣṭa, kāphi alla} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{mūḷe}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಒಂದು} do in front of a noun you are not counting? (It works like the English \emph{a}.) Does Kannada have an article? (No.)
\end{tcolorbox}
